+  abstract: Personalized LLM agents rely on an agent harness, the surrounding memory and control code, to connect
+    user history with downstream decisions. Existing methods typically employ either a single shared memory workflow
+    across all users, which is efficient to deploy but cannot adapt how evidence is retrieved and interpreted across
+    diverse histories, or per-user harness optimization, which customizes behavior for each user but requires costly
+    repeated candidate evaluation at deployment and suffers from sparse, noisy supervision in raw logs. To address
+    this trade-off, we present HyperHarness, a framework that learns a shared history-to-harness generator to synthesize
+    executable, user-specific retrieval and answer-guidance code directly from user histories. Given a user's permitted
+    history, HyperHarness prompts a construction LLM to write personalized retrieval and guidance functions, while
+    downstream task scores across training users supervise iterative refinements to the shared generator without
+    reference harnesses or answering-model updates. At deployment, the frozen generator constructs a harness for
+    each unseen user in a single pass from history alone, eliminating per-user task-scored search. Across three
+    benchmarks (PersonaMemv3, Mem-PAL, and MemoryCD) and three answering models (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.8-27B, and GPT-5.6-Luna),
+    HyperHarness achieves the highest aggregate score in seven of nine settings and ranks second in the remaining
+    two, improving over the strongest baselines by up to 5.95 points while cutting matched answer-time tokens by
+    90.32% over long-context prompting. Analyses show that optimization tailors context allocation to each executor,
+    transfers to unseen user clusters, and amortizes adaptation costs.

+  announced: '2026-11-21'

+  abstract: Collaborative agents joining an ongoing team rely on shared context to connect multi-party interaction
+    histories with downstream coordination decisions. Existing work typically focuses either on retrieving historical
+    facts from conversation logs, which surfaces isolated evidence without capturing who knows or owns what, or
+    on evaluating end-to-end interactions, which conflates preparation with execution and lacks direct supervision
+    because a team's history has no single ground-truth summary. To bridge this gap, we formulate group briefing,
+    the task of reconstructing task-relevant group cognition across participants' expressed beliefs, group dynamics,
+    and grounding gaps, and introduce a four-domain benchmark of 1,351 requests and 9,975 verified reference points
+    paired with a two-stage evaluation pipeline combining reference-point coverage and downstream collaboration
+    simulation. Using this pipeline, we show that GroupBrief, a simple task-guided approach that iteratively probes
+    the message history and synthesizes a structured brief without offline memory indexing or graph construction,
+    outperforms ten retrieval and agent-memory baselines in overall coverage with gpt-5.4-mini, while benchmarking
+    nine language models reveals that prospective friction remains harder to recover than past state across model
+    scales. We further use reference-point coverage as a feedback signal for harness optimization, refining GroupBrief's
+    retrieval and synthesis instructions while keeping model weights frozen. On held-out Test projects, GroupBrief
+    (optimized) improves coverage by 2.54 percentage points for gpt-5.4-mini and 12.88 for gpt-5.6-luna, achieving
+    64.46% and 68.42% preference over no brief in downstream simulations. These results establish our benchmark
+    and evaluation pipeline as a foundation for measuring and optimizing how collaborative agents ground in group
+    cognition.
